More specifically cooling, particularly in hotter climates or for energy intensive applications, like data centers, can comprise between 10-30% of the total energy use. These cooling systems are largely comprised of compressor-based direct expansion systems and chilled water systems that use refrigerants or water, respectively, to reject heat. . Electrocaloric (EC) cycles present an eco-friendly alternative to these conventional processes. To activate these cycles, materials must be exposed to a high strength electric field that in polarizes the structure of a material so that it can absorb and release heat. One of the most effective form factors for EC materials are thin films since electrodes, which are applied to both sides of the film, are close and therefore electric field strengths are high. This requires the development of defect free films that will not short or exhibit dielectric breakdown. The manufacturing process itself must also be scalable to ensure that it can be applied to typical HVAC system components (such as ducts) and integrate into HVAC systems. This project introduced electrospray (ES) as a manufacturing process for thin film electrocaloric materials. Working with a specific polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) terpolymer with demonstrated EC properties, we electrosprayed thin polymer films and characterized them for their thickness, morphology, dialectric breakdown strength, and temperature lift (an indication of a film’s ability to increase in temperature under an electric field). The resulting films exhibit superior thickness control, a smoother surfaces, and improved thermal and electrical properties compared to solution casting (SC). Electrosprayed films also are conformal, meaning that they are defect free, because of the electrical charge that must dissipate during processing. This means that any gaps in the film are filled automatically by the charged droplets. The films thus exhibited 100 MV/m or greater breakdown strength. 4 DE-EE0009099 We also found post-annealing of the films at 120˚C enhances the thermal and EC performance, with films achieving a temperature change (ΔT) of 3.6˚C at 100 MV/m when tested near room temperature. This work was published in Cell Reports Physical Sciences. We further explore the incorporation of liquid crystals into the thin films. Liquid crystals (LCs) have been shown to exhibit electrocaloric behavior, but they cannot be formed into films where they can be used under electric fields. Our goal was to incorporate LCs into these films to enhance the electrocaloric effect.
